one_liner: Unlicensed 2016 mirror of Trevor Herselman's 2014 SSE2 memcpy/memmove with CPUID dispatch. Claims to beat the C library but ships no numbers.
what_it_does: Provides apex_memcpy and apex_memmove (apex::memcpy and apex::memmove in the C++ copy), which are global function pointers with the memcpy signature. The first call goes through a dispatcher that reads CPUID leaf 1 and rebinds both pointers to one of three variants: kryptonite on SSE4.2 CPUs, tiberium on SSSE3 CPUs or any x86-64 CPU without SSE4.2, and mithril on 32-bit SSE2-only CPUs. Everything else falls back to the C library. memcpy and memmove share the same routine, so both are overlap-safe. Callers must call apex_memcpy explicitly; nothing interposes the libc symbols.
how_it_is_fast: Copies of 112 bytes or less go through a branch tree with no loop. It loads every 16-byte SSE2 block plus an overlapping 8- or 16-byte tail before it stores anything, so a single path handles overlap. Larger copies use a 64-byte loop (tiberium) or a 32-byte loop (kryptonite) of unaligned SSE2 loads and stores, counting a negative offset up to zero. At 256 KiB and above, the copy aligns the destination to 16 bytes and prefetches 4 KiB ahead with _MM_HINT_NTA. It then writes with non-temporal _mm_stream_si128 stores, running forward or backward depending on overlap. No AVX, ERMS or rep movsb path exists.
when_to_use: Studying a compact C-intrinsics design for overlap-safe small copies: load-everything-then-store branch trees for sizes 0-112 bytes.
Benchmarking against the CPUs it was tuned on (2014-era Core i, Core 2, Pentium 4), or keeping its history in a memcpy survey.
Copying ideas into your own licensed code after independent testing; copying the files themselves is not possible because the mirror carries no license (see status note).
when_not_to_use: Any production use. No license, no tests and no benchmark are in the repository, and the tiberium variant has the out-of-bounds write described under gotchas.
Modern CPUs with AVX2, AVX-512, ERMS or FSRM. The code is SSE2-only, and current libc memcpy implementations use wider vectors and rep movsb, which this code predates.
Copies between 256 KiB and a few MB whose destination is read right afterwards. The 256 KiB non-temporal threshold is hard-coded, so such copies bypass the cache.
Small fixed-size copies (struct copies, memcpy-based type punning). An indirect call through a function pointer replaces what the compiler would otherwise inline as a single move.
Non-x86 targets, where it only forwards to libc memcpy and memmove.

integration.dependencies: none (emmintrin.h plus cpuid.h or intrin.h from the compiler)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (long long, declarations in for loops) or C++ with long long; MSVC, GCC or Clang for the CPUID path; other x86-64 compilers always get tiberium
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 with SSE2; any other architecture falls back to the C library
integration.thread_safety: Copy routines are stateless. The first call's dispatcher writes the two global function pointers without atomics, a formal data race when several threads make their first call at once (each thread writes the same value).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same signature and return value, but different names called through function pointers; libc memcpy and memmove are not replaced, and memcpy also pays memmove's direction check

gotchas: Correctness bug found by reading the code; it was not run, since building is outside this task. In tiberium's backward (overlapping, dst > src) path for 113 bytes to 256 KiB, `size = -size;` runs before the `size > 32` and `size > 48` tests (apex_memmove.c lines 377-382, apex_memmove.cpp lines 379-382). size is an unsigned size_t, so both tests always pass. When n mod 64 is 17-47, the tail loads from src-32 and src-48 and stores to dst-32 and dst-48 relative to the 17-47-byte remainder. That writes up to 31 bytes before dst and reads up to 31 bytes before src. Example: memmove(buf+10, buf, 150) overwrites buf[0..9] (source bytes outside the destination) and the 16 bytes before buf with the bytes that lie 10 positions earlier. kryptonite and mithril test before negating and are not affected. tiberium runs on x86-64 CPUs without SSE4.2 (Core 2, AMD K8/K10), on 32-bit SSSE3-only CPUs, and on every x86-64 build from a compiler other than MSVC, GCC or Clang.

Copies of 256 KiB and up use _mm_stream_si128 non-temporal stores and never issue _mm_sfence (no sfence appears anywhere in the source). Another thread that sees a later ordinary flag store may still read stale destination data.

Unaligned accesses through casts to long long*, int* and short* are formally undefined behaviour under C alignment and strict-aliasing rules. They work on x86 with current compilers, but sanitizers will flag them.
The .c and .cpp files are near-identical copies (the C++ one adds namespace apex). A fix to one must be repeated in the other.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely. Agner Fog's asmlib and DPDK's rte_memcpy are x86 copy routines with documented measurements against glibc, and AOCL-LibMem covers AMD Zen with a benchmark tool. Pick apex-memmove only as a short, readable C-intrinsics reference for overlap-safe SSE2 small-size copies.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing is measured in the repository. The README says only 'The fastest memcpy/memmove on x86/x64 ... EVER (according to the author)'. The CodeProject article with the original methodology does not resolve from here, nor does the PostgreSQL 2016 thread where Alvaro Herrera asked for real-workload gains. The only number known, 3.55 ms vs 4.37 ms against the MSVC CRT memcpy in one Core i7 run, comes from a search snippet of a 2020 Ultimate++ forum post (snippet only, block size and flags unknown).
status_note: Abandoned mirror (three commits, all on 2016-09-22, 14 stars, no issues filed). It is reference only: the mirror carries no license, and a PostgreSQL list post (search snippet only) says the CodeProject original is under the Code Project Open License. Its tiberium variant also has an out-of-bounds write on backward overlapping moves.
